name: Priya Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Marsh & Daughters, an eight-person firm above a pharmacy on the high street. Our clients are shopkeepers, a few landlords, two dentists and a dry cleaner who still brings his receipts in a biscuit tin. I prepare their year-end accounts and personal tax returns, and I do it the way I was trained: the spreadsheet, the ticks in the margin, a phone call when something looks odd.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing my clients. Mr Okafor at the dry cleaner rings me before he buys anything over £500, and I like being that person for him. What wears me out is new software, honestly. Every time the firm changes a system I lose a week, and I've never touched any of the AI tools the younger staff talk about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that accounting has always been about judgement, not just typing numbers in. I'm not really an online person, so I'd say it to my colleague Joan over lunch. We'd have a little laugh about all the fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a relief. I've got savings, I own my flat, and my job is steady, so if nothing changes I'm in a good spot. I never wanted to learn the AI tools at my accounting firm, and in this version I'd never have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, and maybe finally ask for a pay review, since I've been there five years. I'd keep paying extra into the mortgage on my flat, about £300 a month. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit smug, if I'm honest, which isn't a very nice feeling to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Marsh, who owns the firm, is 66, and nobody knows what happens when she retires. If a bigger firm buys us, they'll bring their own systems. That worries me more than AI does, in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a bigger firm did buy Marsh & Daughters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay and learn their system, slowly and grumbling. There are plenty of firms around here, so I could move, but I'd rather not start again with new people.

say: Accounting has always been about **judgement**, not just typing in numbers.
All the **fuss** about AI was overblown, and I'd laugh about it over lunch.
think: It's a **relief**, because I never wanted to learn the AI tools.
With savings, my **own flat** and a steady job, I'm in a good spot.
do: Ask Mrs Marsh for a **pay review** after five years at the firm.
Keep paying an extra **£300 a month** off the mortgage on my flat.
feel: A little **smug**, which she admits isn't a nice feeling.
S0.quote: I never wanted to learn the AI tools at my accounting firm, and in this version I'd never have to.
fieldNote: Priya's **security** is real: savings, her own flat and plenty of firms nearby.
Her existing worry is the owner's **retirement** and a possible takeover, not AI.
She openly enjoys being proved right, which says a lot about her **dislike of change**.

steps.text: Keep preparing accounts the usual way and ask for a pay review
Pay an extra £300 a month off her flat's mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should be careful, because clients trust us with their money and a computer can't sit across a desk from them. To friends I'd say I'll get on with it. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm exactly the person who gets left behind. I don't use any of these tools, and the work I do, checking and preparing returns, is what the card says goes first. My accounting firm would hire a graduate who uses AI before they'd wait for me to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off at first and see what Mrs Marsh decides, because she's no faster with technology than me. I'd build my savings up from eight months to a full year, by cutting the extra mortgage payments. If the firm made us learn the tools, I'd go on the course, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like being the last one in the class who still doesn't get long division.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get on with it, and also that you'd be left behind. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd get on with it in public and lie awake about it at home. I'm good at looking calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most if the tax returns moved to software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone calls. When Mr Okafor's numbers look odd, I ring him and it turns out he bought a new steam press. I don't know how software has that conversation.

say: We should be **careful**, because clients trust us with their money.
I'd **get on with it** and keep quiet online.
think: I'm the one who gets **left behind**, because I've never used these tools.
The firm would rather hire a **graduate who uses AI** than wait for me.
do: Wait to see what **Mrs Marsh decides** before changing anything.
Build savings from eight months to **a full year** by pausing extra mortgage payments.
Go on a **training course** only if the firm makes it compulsory.
feel: **Anxious**, like the last one in class who doesn't understand.
S1.quote: My accounting firm would hire a graduate who uses AI before they'd wait for me to catch up.
fieldNote: Priya's work is **high-exposure** checking and returns, and she knows it.
There's a clear gap between her **calm public face** and her sleepless private worry.
She'd only learn the tools **under pressure**, which fits her resistance to change.

steps.text: Wait for Mrs Marsh's decision before changing how she works
Pause extra mortgage payments and build savings to twelve months
Attend the firm's AI tools course if it becomes compulsory

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that the government needs to slow it down. At work I'd ask Mrs Marsh straight out what it means for us. I'd probably tell my parents I'm fine, though I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone within a couple of years. Everything I do is at a desk, so it goes on the first date. I'm 27 and I've only ever been an accountant, so I don't know what else I'm for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop every extra spend: no new car, no holiday, nothing. I'd keep a year of costs in cash and talk to my dad, who runs a small catering business, about whether there's work there. I'd look at jobs that need a person in a room, maybe the front desk of a dental practice I already do the books for, even if it pays less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and a bit numb. I keep thinking I chose a safe career on purpose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm fine and that I've got savings, which is true. I wouldn't tell them I'd been looking at catering jobs at my dad's place, because he'd worry I'd thrown my degree away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would hands-on work feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots are three years behind, aren't they? That's three years of wages, and maybe more if people still want a person serving them. It's not a plan, it's just somewhere to stand.

say: It's **frightening**, and the government needs to **slow it down**.
I'd ask Mrs Marsh **straight out** what it means for the firm.
think: My job is **gone** within a couple of years, because it's all **desk work**.
I've only been an accountant and **don't know what else** I'm for.
do: Cut **every extra spend**, including the new car and holidays.
Keep **a year of costs** in cash.
Ask her dad about work at his **catering business** or a dental front desk.
feel: **Scared** and numb, after choosing a **safe career** on purpose.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and I've only ever been an accountant, so I don't know what else I'm for.
fieldNote: Priya expects to **lose her job** and has no appetite for a new kind of work.
She'd lean on **family** quietly while telling her parents she's fine.
Hands-on work appeals only as **somewhere to stand** for three more years, not as a plan.

steps.text: Cancel the new car and holidays for the first year
Hold a full year of living costs in cash
Apply for a front-desk job at a dental practice client
Ask her dad about shifts at his catering business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short and people like me need help to change. At work I'd start asking which jobs at the firm would still exist. I still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending as the fast one, I just get to see it coming. I'd be 32, with more saved and the flat paid down more. Five years is long enough for me to dread AGI, and maybe not long enough for me to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, probably £600 a month, because the pay is good while it lasts. In year two or three I'd look into a part-time course in something with people in it, maybe bookkeeping for small charities face to face, or even dental nursing. I'd want to see what others did first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the two-year one. More of a slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see what others do. What if they're waiting too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're all stuck, aren't we? I know I'm slow. I'd probably need a push, like the firm announcing a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good last day at the firm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Handing Mr Okafor's biscuit tin back and telling him who'll look after him now. Saying a proper goodbye, not getting an email.

say: Five years is **short**, and people like me need **help to change**.
I'd ask at work which jobs at the firm will **still exist**.
think: It's the **same ending** as the fast one, only seen coming.
Five years may not be **long enough** for someone as slow to change as me.
do: Save about **£600 a month** while the pay lasts.
Look into a **part-time course** in dental nursing or face-to-face bookkeeping by year three.
feel: **Anxious**, as a slow worry rather than panic.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to dread AGI, and maybe not long enough for me to change.
fieldNote: The extra time eases Priya's fear only a little, because she knows she **changes slowly**.
She'd wait for **others to move first**, and admits she may need a firm deadline.
Her idea of a good exit is a **proper goodbye** to clients, which shows what she values.

steps.text: Save about £600 a month while the firm still pays well
Watch what colleagues do before choosing a new path
Enrol in a part-time dental nursing course by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty and we shouldn't panic. To Joan I'd say we'll both be fine. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels far off, and I know that's dangerous for someone like me. I'll tell myself 2036 is ages away, and then wake up at 36 with a job a computer does better. Like I said with the slower one, my problem isn't money, it's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Marsh & Daughters and keep paying the flat down, so by my mid-thirties I owe very little. I'd tell myself I'll retrain in year five. If I'm honest, I'd probably need my sister to nag me into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then anxious when I think about it properly. Mostly I'd try not to think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would nag you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger sister Amira, she's a nurse and she's always on at me to try new things. She'd sign me up for something and send me the link.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually retrain in, given ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably something hands-on with people, because the robots come later. Dental nursing still appeals, because I already know the practice I do the books for.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and there's no need to **panic**.
My colleague Joan and I will **both be fine**.
think: Ten years feels **far off**, which is dangerous for someone like me.
do: Keep working at **Marsh & Daughters** and pay the flat down hard.
Plan to **retrain** in about year five, with her sister **Amira** pushing her.
S4.quote: I'll tell myself 2036 is ages away, and then wake up at 36 with a job a computer does better.
fieldNote: Priya knows ten years tempts her to **put things off**, and says so plainly.
She has strong **savings** but expects her job to **end by 2036**.
Her sister **Amira** is her real plan, which shows how much she relies on family.

steps.text: Stay at Marsh & Daughters preparing accounts for regular clients
Overpay the flat mortgage so little is owed by her mid-thirties
Let her sister Amira sign her up for a retraining course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028. I'd have the money to survive but nowhere to go, and I'm not quick. What would help is someone sitting me down and showing me, step by step, what jobs exist and how to get there, with a real person, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. People like Mr Okafor (her dry-cleaning client) will be just as lost as me, and nobody's asking about them either. I'd worry about him more than me, honestly.

headlineQuote: People like Mr Okafor (her dry-cleaning client) will be just as lost as me, and nobody's asking about them either.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old accountant** at a small high-street firm who has never used AI tools.
She owns her flat, has **eight months saved** and knows her clients personally.
She's **calm** if AI stalls, but expects to **lose her job** in every AGI picture.
Her problem isn't money but **changing course**, and she admits she'd wait for a push.
She leans on **family**, especially her sister Amira, and worries about her older clients.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have money to survive but nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: A **real person** guiding her step by step through which jobs exist and how to reach them.
